title: Functional interpretation of GWAS · Monday, November 23

transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Functional interpretation of GWAS, for Monday, November 23.
Let's turn to Functional interpretation of GWAS.
We have one paper today, a bioRxiv preprint from the Jiang lab called EPIC2. It asks a familiar question: which cell types actually matter for a given trait?

Their approach combines GWAS summary statistics with single-cell chromatin accessibility data. The idea is to test whether the strength of GWAS association tracks with how accessible the chromatin is in specific cell types.
Importantly, the test accounts for linkage disequilibrium. Without that, you can get inflated signal just because a few correlated variants sit in open chromatin.

They also run the test at two resolutions, individual SNPs and regulatory peaks. Then they merge the two p-values with a Cauchy combination test, which stays valid even when the two tests are correlated.
That's a nice design choice. SNP-level resolution can catch sharp signals, and peak-level aggregation can pick up diffuse ones, so you don't have to commit to either in advance.
On the practical side, it's an R package with vignettes and reproducible test data, so it should be easy to try on our own single-cell ATAC datasets.

One caution, though. The abstract is a software summary, so it reports no benchmarks, no comparisons with existing enrichment methods, and no example traits. And it's a preprint, so we'd want to see calibration and power results before relying on it.
Agreed. The takeaway: EPIC2 is a promising, LD-aware tool for linking GWAS signal to cell types through chromatin accessibility, but its performance still has to be shown.

papers.title: EPIC2: integrating single-cell chromatin accessibility with human genetics to identify trait-relevant cell types
